summary: This standards-track document updates the Java bindings for the Generic Security Services API (GSS-API), which gives programmers a uniform way to use security services across different underlying mechanisms. It revises the earlier Java bindings specification for version 2 of the API.

plainLanguage.summary: Programmers can use one set of buttons to lock and check things, whatever lock is inside. This updates the Java version of those buttons.

questions: what are the java bindings for gss-api
how to use gss-api version 2 from java
subtitle: The Java classes and methods for GSS-API version 2, now able to return an error token to the peer.

tldr.problem: Programmers need one uniform way to authenticate peers and protect messages across different security mechanisms. The earlier Java bindings (RFC 5653) could return a token or throw an exception on failure, but never both, so a failure could not be reported to the peer.
tldr.mechanism: The org.ietf.jgss package defines classes such as GSSManager, GSSName, GSSCredential and GSSContext. A new output token field in GSSException lets initSecContext and acceptSecContext hand back an error token when they fail.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8353 obsoletes RFC 5653 and removes the stream-based GSSContext methods.

today: RFC 8353 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2018. It obsoletes RFC 5653 and, per the unit metadata, has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Java Bindings for the GSS-API
sections.content:
This document specifies Java language bindings for version 2 of the Generic Security Services Application Programming Interface (GSS-API), which RFC 2743 describes in a language-independent way. The GSS-API lets an application authenticate a principal identity, delegate rights to a peer, and apply confidentiality and integrity to individual messages. It sits on top of mechanisms such as the Kerberos version 5 mechanism (RFC 4121).

The bindings follow the work in RFC 2853 and RFC 5653 and draw on the C bindings in RFC 2744. They aim to be object oriented. They also serve both applications that use a system-wide implementation and those that bundle a custom one. Mechanisms are pluggable through the Java Cryptography Architecture (JCA) provider model.
sections.plainLanguage: Many different locks exist, but this gives programmers one set of buttons that works with all of them. This book explains the buttons for people who write programs in Java.

sections.title: The Four Stages of Using GSS-API
sections.content:
The RFC describes four stages. First, the application acquires credentials to prove its identity. Second, a pair of applications establishes a joint security context, which holds shared state such as cryptographic keys and message sequence numbers. Third, per-message services protect application data. Fourth, each side releases the context when the session is over.

Establishing a context is driven by the application. The initiator calls initSecContext and the acceptor calls acceptSecContext. Each call may produce a token that the application must carry to its peer. isEstablished() returns false while more tokens are needed. It is possible for a call to return a token and for isEstablished() to be true, which means the token must still be sent but the local end is complete.

For per-message protection, getMIC produces a checksum token that the peer checks with verifyMIC, along with the message. wrap places the message and its protection inside one token, optionally encrypting, and the peer calls unwrap. When finished, the application SHOULD call dispose.
sections.plainLanguage: First you get an ID card. Then you and a friend swap secret notes until you both trust each other. Then you send protected messages. At the end you tear up the secret notes.

sections.title: Optional Services and Controls
sections.content:
Before the first init call, the context initiator may request optional services using methods on GSSContext. Only the initiator can request them. The RFC lists delegation, mutual authentication, replay detection, out-of-sequence detection and anonymous authentication. After establishment, query methods report what the context actually provides, which might not match the request. If a missing property is necessary for the application protocol, the application SHOULD destroy the context.

For delegation, if the application says delegation is not desired, the implementation MUST NOT allow it. The acceptor can use getCredDelegState and getDelegCred to obtain the delegated credential. For anonymity, the acceptor sees a reserved internal name, and comparing it with equals MUST return false.

Contexts can be moved between processes on one machine with export and a byte-array constructor. The resulting inter-process token MAY contain sensitive data such as keys, so applications MUST protect it in transit. Implementations are not required to support transfer, and isTransferable reports whether it works.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you start, you can ask for extras, like having your friend show their ID too, or hiding your own name. Some locks cannot do every extra, so you check afterwards what you really got.

sections.title: Classes and Interfaces in org.ietf.jgss
sections.content:
All classes live in the package org.ietf.jgss. Numeric values use the Java int type, tokens are byte arrays, and text uses String.

  • GSSManager: an abstract factory for names, credentials and contexts. It also reports which mechanisms and name types are available. A default instance comes from getInstance().
  • GSSName: an interface for names. It defines standard name-type OIDs such as NT_HOSTBASED_SERVICE, NT_USER_NAME and NT_ANONYMOUS. Names can be compared, canonicalized into a mechanism name and exported.
  • GSSCredential: an interface for credentials, which may hold several mechanism-specific elements. Usage constants are INITIATE_AND_ACCEPT (0), INITIATE_ONLY (1) and ACCEPT_ONLY (2).
  • GSSContext: an interface for context establishment and the per-message services.
  • MessageProp, ChannelBinding, Oid and GSSException: helper classes for message properties, channel bindings, object identifiers and errors.

Java's garbage collection removes the need for several RFC 2743 routines, such as the ones that release names or build object identifier sets. Implementations find mechanisms through providers, and addProviderAtFront and addProviderAtEnd let an application choose a provider for one GSSManager instance. How providers are located is left to a separate Service Provider Interface specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The toolbox has a few main tools: one that makes things, one for names, one for ID cards and one for the secret conversation. Each does one job.

sections.title: Errors and the Output Token
sections.content:
Fatal errors are reported by throwing GSSException, which carries a major (GSS-level) code, a mechanism-specific minor code (0 means none) and text for both. If an exception occurs during context establishment, the context negotiation has failed and the GSSContext MUST be abandoned. In a per-message call the context MAY remain usable.

Informational conditions in verifyMIC and unwrap are not exceptions. They are reported through the MessageProp object with isDuplicateToken, isOldToken, isUnseqToken and isGapToken, and the application decides what to do. The same four conditions become fatal exceptions only if they occur during context establishment.

The key change in this RFC is that a GSSException MAY include an output token that SHOULD be sent to the peer. The new five-argument constructor accepts one, and getOutputToken() returns a copy. The value MUST be null if there is no token and MUST NOT be an empty array. After a failed initSecContext or acceptSecContext, callers SHOULD check it and send any token to the other side.
sections.plainLanguage: If something goes wrong, the program shouts an alarm. Now the alarm can also carry a little note for the other side that explains what happened.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The section concerns the Java security model rather than the cryptography. When a Java security manager is in use, application code runs in a sandbox, and administrators decide which permissions to give. A Kerberos provider might need a network connection to the Key Distribution Center, which the sandbox would block unless permission is granted. This checking is transparent to the application and outside the scope of the RFC.

If an application needs a particular provider, it has two choices. It can install the provider JVM-wide through java.security.Security, which requires the insertProvider SecurityPermission, or it can pass the provider to its own GSSManager instance, which needs no permissions. The RFC also warns that inter-process tokens may contain key material and must be protected in transit.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs often play inside a fenced yard. If a lock needs to call a far-off helper, a grown-up must first open the gate.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 5653
sections.content:
Two things changed compared with RFC 5653. First, the design flaw: a Java method can return a token or throw an exception, but not both. The C bindings can return a status and an output token together. Without a way to emit an error token, a Java application could not send, for example, a reject NegTokenResp token for the SPNEGO mechanism (RFC 4178). The fix embeds the token in the exception. New programs SHOULD use it but are not required to, and a program meant to run on both old and new bindings can use reflection to check whether getOutputToken exists.

Second, the overloaded stream-based methods of GSSContext for initSecContext, acceptSecContext, wrap, unwrap, getMIC and verifyMIC are removed. The stated reasons are that the wire protocol should be defined by an application, not a library, and that these methods cannot be implemented correctly when tokens have no self-framing or the library does not know the token format.

The RFC also keeps the changes from RFC 2853, such as defining numeric values for the major status codes, which had been misaligned between deployed implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The old design could hand you a note or shout an alarm, but never both. Now the alarm can carry the note. A few older shortcuts for sending notes were taken out.
